title: Arson hits 22 Grameen Bank branches; UN calls for investigation
excerpt: Grameen Bank says 22 branches in 16 districts were set on fire or targeted between 10 and 17 November. The UN says all violence should be investigated.
content:
Arsonists have set fire to or tried to burn 22 Grameen Bank branches in 16 districts between 10 and 17 November, the bank said in a statement on 17 November. It warned that the attacks threaten financial services for the low-income and marginalised people it serves.

The branches are in Sherpur, Cox's Bazar, Madaripur, Dinajpur, Naogaon, Patuakhali, Noakhali, Chattogram, Pabna, Nilphamari, Netrokona, Kishoreganj, Gazipur, Sylhet, Gopalganj and Rangpur. On 15 November the Ulpur branch in Gopalganj was vandalised and set on fire, with CCTV cameras and monitors destroyed and a hard drive reportedly taken. The same day, an arson attack reportedly destroyed nearly all of the Patgati branch office in Tungipara.

The bank said damage to equipment and records can disrupt services for women entrepreneurs, small business owners, farmers and other members, and puts at risk the savings and livelihoods of millions of people. It also said misleading information about its ownership and operations was spreading on social media, and asked people to check facts with a branch or an authorised representative.

Grameen Bank has more than 10.67 million members, 2,528 branches and works in 81,678 villages, according to its October 2026 report.

UN response

Asked about the attacks at a briefing in New York on 16 November, Farhan Haq, Deputy Spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General, said: "We believe that all acts of violence should be thoroughly investigated by the national authorities." He added that protesters have the right to protest, but that it must be peaceful.

Grameen Bank was founded by Nobel laureate Dr Muhammad Yunus, who served as chief adviser of the interim government.

Why it matters

Grameen Bank is one of the country's largest microfinance lenders, and most of its members are rural women. Attacks on branches put staff at risk, can destroy loan and savings records, and may push borrowers towards informal moneylenders. Other NGOs and microfinance institutions working in the same districts may also need to review security for field offices and staff.

What to watch

  • Whether police identify and charge those responsible.
  • Whether branches reopen and members can reach their savings.
  • Whether attacks spread to other NGO or microfinance offices.

Sources

  • All acts of violence in Bangladesh should be thoroughly investigated: UN, The Business Standard (UNB), 17 Nov 2026
